accuracy.evidence: Sunrise and sunset times are mid-month London clock times (GMT in winter, BST in summer) checked against HM Nautical Almanac Office / timeanddate.com tables for London: mid-June about 04:43 to 21:21 (16 h 38 min), mid-December about 08:00 to 15:55 (7 h 55 min); the lab's twelve monthly day lengths run from 7.9 h (December) to 16.6 h (June). Monthly warmest-part-of-day temperatures are Met Office 1991-2020 London average daily maxima rounded (8 °C in January and December, 23 °C in July and August). Perihelion in early January and reversed southern seasons were checked against NASA Space Place.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets misconceptions reported by Philips (1991) and the Nuffield SPACE project on children's ideas about day length and seasons: a winter day is shorter than 24 hours (prediction 2, 'short' feedback, p3), summer is warm because the Sun is closer (practice p1, m4, 'close' feedback, adult text), bedtime moves rather than sunset ('clock'), the days keep growing past June (prediction 4, 'keep', p5), and the seasons are the same everywhere (m7, adult text).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdaylen is about the amount of daylight through the year: a window at a fixed 7 pm bedtime that is light or dark depending on the month tile chosen, two 24-box days filled hour by hour for June and December, four month cards that only accept the least-daylight month next, a 12-bar daylight chart revealed by sliding a finger, and a tree plus thermometer driven by the same month tiles. flagsky sorts a day and night sky, drags the Sun from morning to night and spins a season wheel; it has no day-length data. Gate lab_distinct passes under the 30% limit.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child sees the pattern before the text names it: the same 7 pm window turns light only in the spring and summer months; both day strips are 24 boxes yet the light boxes differ about two to one; the month cards refuse any month that is not the darkest one left, so the order winter-to-summer is built by the child; the year chart rises to June and falls back to December once all 12 bars are revealed; the tree and thermometer change only when the month changes.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'always dark' at 7 pm (June is light), 'the same: a day is always 24 hours' (true length, but the light part differs, shown box by box), 'no different' from winter to summer (the ordered bars grow), 'keep getting longer' after June (the chart falls), and 'snowy' or 'colder' for long days (the thermometer reads 23 °C in July).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions with eight distinct feedback messages naming the slip: swapping summer and winter; thinking light hours never change; the Sun coming closer; bedtime rather than sunset moving; a December day being only 8 hours long; daylight growing past June; trees making warmth. Each wrong answer shows the reason and a Next one button for a fresh question.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation reads at FK grade 2.2 with very short sentences and the words season, daylight, light, dark, summer, winter, sunshine; adult text is within the 9.5 limit overall and names the Year 1 and NGSS 1-ESS1-2 aims. Lab steps use one or two short sentences, month initials plus colour bands for non-readers, and the young layout with 56 px buttons; numbers stay at whole or half hours.

no_filler.evidence: Gate finds no filler phrases. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (sunset moves, light hours versus the 24-hour day, the yearly pattern, sunshine and warmth). Items are varied: p2 and m8 compare summer and winter hours, p4 finds dark hours from light hours, m6 counts sunrise to sunset across midday, m5 reasons from walking to school in the dark, m7 checks the southern hemisphere.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark: the twelve month tiles span the canvas width as the drag strip and each is a tap target; window, day strips, month boxes and the year chart fit the 390 px tall layout with labels on white pills; the season labels sit under the chart without clipping; month and fill buttons use 56 px young buttons that wrap to two rows.

accessibility.evidence: Everything on the canvas also has a labelled button: back and forward a month plus Jump to June or July, Fill in June and Fill in December, a button per month card, Show every month and three tallest-month buttons, and the challenge answers. The canvas aria-label states the month, sunset time and result after every action; challenge feedback is a polite live region; walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
